title: Threat Recognition & Attribution
scenario: Analysts flag a wave of social media posts and articles pushing the claim that a neighbouring country's government is illegitimate and its population isn't a distinct nation. The claim is repeated by several outlets that appear editorially independent of each other.
question: How do you classify and respond to this activity?
learnMore: Russian information operations run on 'grand narratives' — big, slow-built ideological frames repeated across many channels — rather than on individual false stories. A single fake headline rarely does lasting damage; a grand narrative repeated for years does.

options.text: Flag it as a coordinated grand narrative campaign and brief media literacy partners on the underlying historical claim, not just the individual posts
options.summary: Identified and briefed on a coordinated grand narrative campaign.

options.text: Fact-check each individual post as unrelated misinformation with no broader pattern
options.summary: Treated the campaign as isolated misinformation posts.

options.text: Ignore it since no single post contains verifiably false information
options.summary: Took no action on the emerging narrative campaign.

options.text: Demand the platforms remove all the posts immediately without further analysis
options.summary: Ordered immediate takedown without analysis.

title: Threat Recognition & Attribution
scenario: Your agency's monitoring picks up unusual traffic patterns hitting several bank and government websites simultaneously. It's not yet clear if this is a technical glitch, a coincidence, or a deliberate attack.
question: What's your first move?
learnMore: Estonia's 2007 crisis began exactly this way — distributed denial of service attacks flooding banks, media, and government pages until they crashed. Early, correct recognition that this was a deliberate cyber-attack shaped the entire government response that followed.

options.text: Convene technical teams immediately to confirm whether this is a coordinated denial-of-service attack before making any public statement
options.summary: Convened technical teams to confirm a possible coordinated attack.

options.text: Assume it's a routine technical issue and wait for it to resolve on its own
options.summary: Assumed the traffic spike was a routine technical issue.

options.text: Publicly announce a cyber-attack immediately, before technical confirmation
options.summary: Announced a cyber-attack before technical confirmation.

options.text: Take the affected sites offline preemptively without investigating first
options.summary: Took sites offline preemptively without investigation.

title: Institutional Coordination
scenario: Cybersecurity responsibility in your government has drifted across several ministries over the years with no single clear owner. You're asked to recommend where primary ministerial purview should sit.
question: What do you recommend?
learnMore: Estonia's ministerial responsibility for cybersecurity has shifted more than once — from the Ministry of Defence, to the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (to prioritise the private-sector relationship), to a dedicated Justice and Digital Affairs Ministry. There's no single governmental ministry for cybersecurity in most countries — responsibility is typically split.

options.text: Establish a clear primary ministerial purview while keeping cross-ministry coordination channels active — no single ministry can own it alone
options.summary: Established clear primary purview with active cross-ministry coordination.

options.text: Leave responsibility informally distributed across ministries with no clear lead
options.summary: Left cybersecurity responsibility informally distributed.

options.text: Centralise all cybersecurity decisions in a single ministry with no coordination mechanism for others
options.summary: Centralised cybersecurity in a single ministry with no coordination.

options.text: Create a new ministry solely for cybersecurity from scratch immediately
options.summary: Created a standalone cybersecurity ministry immediately.

title: Institutional Coordination
scenario: Your country must comply with the EU's NIS2 Directive on Cybersecurity. Some agencies already meet several of its requirements; others are starting from near zero.
question: How do you sequence compliance work?
learnMore: NIS2 applies to all EU member states, but compliance difficulty varies a lot — in Estonia's case, many of NIS2's parameters were already in place, making compliance comparatively easy. Countries starting from scratch face a much steeper climb.

options.text: Audit which agencies are closest to compliance, prioritise resources toward the gaps, and use already-compliant agencies as internal models
options.summary: Sequenced NIS2 compliance work based on an internal audit.

options.text: Apply the exact same compliance timeline uniformly across every agency regardless of starting point
options.summary: Applied a uniform NIS2 compliance timeline to all agencies.

options.text: Focus only on agencies already close to compliance and deprioritise the rest
options.summary: Focused NIS2 efforts only on already-compliant agencies.

options.text: Delay all NIS2 compliance work until a future budget cycle
options.summary: Delayed all NIS2 compliance work.

title: Countering Narratives
scenario: A self-described 'independent human rights expert' has been giving testimony at international meetings claiming your country's school reforms amount to 'language genocide' against a minority group — a term with no basis in international law. His travel is quietly funded by a foreign embassy.
question: How do you counter this?
learnMore: This mirrors the real Seredenko case in Estonia: a supposedly independent voice, financed by a foreign embassy, whose claims were then cited back by that country's own officials as evidence — a technique sometimes called 'source washing,' where a narrative is laundered through an apparently independent mouthpiece.

options.text: Publicly document the funding link and the term's absence in international law, and brief allied delegations before the next international meeting
options.summary: Exposed the funding link and briefed allies ahead of time.

options.text: Publicly denounce the individual personally without addressing the funding or the substance of the claim
options.summary: Denounced the individual personally without addressing substance.

options.text: Say nothing publicly and hope the claim doesn't gain traction
options.summary: Took no public action against the narrative.

options.text: Attempt to have the individual barred from all future international meetings
options.summary: Attempted to bar the individual from international meetings.

title: Countering Narratives
scenario: A local NGO with unclear funding sources begins organising protests, framing them as a spontaneous grassroots reaction to a recent policy change. Intelligence suggests the organising activity has links to a foreign intelligence service.
question: How do you handle this?
learnMore: This mirrors the 'amplifying internal conflicts' stage of the Gerasimov doctrine: existing social tensions are exploited and organised protest activity is used to polarise society and destabilise trust in institutions, often while appearing organic.

options.text: Continue lawful monitoring of the organising activity while protecting the right to genuine protest, and prepare public information on the policy change itself
options.summary: Monitored the activity lawfully while protecting genuine protest rights.

options.text: Ban the protest outright to prevent any risk of foreign-linked organising
options.summary: Banned the protest outright.

options.text: Publicly accuse the NGO of foreign coordination before the intelligence assessment is confirmed
options.summary: Made public accusations before the assessment was confirmed.

options.text: Take no action of any kind and treat it as an unrelated domestic matter
options.summary: Treated the organising activity as unrelated to foreign interference.

title: Public Communication
scenario: A confirmed cyber-attack is disrupting government and bank websites. Advisors are split: some want to downplay the incident to avoid public panic, others want to disclose it fully and immediately.
question: How do you communicate about the ongoing incident?
learnMore: A common factor across Estonia's 2007 and 2017 crises was radical transparency: clear, deliberate public acknowledgment of the attack, paired with continuous, honest communication — this approach was credited with maintaining public calm rather than fuelling panic.

options.text: Publicly and clearly acknowledge the attack is happening, with regular honest updates as the picture develops
options.summary: Communicated with radical transparency throughout the incident.

options.text: Downplay the incident publicly to avoid causing panic, while working on it quietly behind the scenes
options.summary: Downplayed the incident publicly.

options.text: Say nothing publicly until the incident is fully resolved
options.summary: Withheld public comment until full resolution.

options.text: Immediately blame a specific foreign government publicly before attribution is confirmed
options.summary: Publicly blamed a foreign government before confirming attribution.

title: Public Communication
scenario: War memorials in several towns are found vandalised with symbols designed to make it look like domestic extremist groups are responsible, aiming to suggest your own society is harbouring the very ideology it claims to oppose.
question: How do you communicate about this to the public?
learnMore: This mirrors real 2023–24 GRU-linked cases in Estonia: recruited locals were instructed to stage vandalism designed to look like domestic extremism, with the deeper aim of creating fear, instability, and mistrust in government — while making the incidents look like organic domestic protest.

options.text: Explain publicly what investigators have found so far about the staged nature of the vandalism, without waiting for the full case to close
options.summary: Explained the staged nature of the vandalism as it was uncovered.

options.text: Let the vandalism speak for itself with no government statement
options.summary: Made no public statement about the vandalism.

options.text: Publicly declare it a case of genuine domestic extremism before the investigation concludes
options.summary: Declared it domestic extremism before the investigation concluded.

options.text: Restrict media coverage of the incidents entirely to avoid amplifying them
options.summary: Restricted media coverage of the incidents.

title: Crisis Response
scenario: The denial-of-service attack from earlier has escalated: bank, media, and government sites are now intermittently unreachable nationwide, and public frustration is rising fast.
question: What's your response during the live incident?
learnMore: Estonia's 2007 response combined clear recognition of the attack, radical transparency in communication, and continuous technical mitigation — a combination credited with preventing the crisis from escalating into wider public panic.

options.text: Activate technical mitigation teams, maintain honest public updates on progress, and coordinate with banks and media on service restoration priorities
options.summary: Activated coordinated mitigation with transparent public updates.

news.headline: Coordinated Response Restores Services Within Hours
news.content: Banks and government sites came back online in stages as mitigation teams worked through the night. Officials credited close coordination and steady public communication with preventing wider disruption, though some smaller banks reported lingering outages.

options.text: Focus resources only on government sites and leave banks and media to handle their own mitigation
options.summary: Focused mitigation only on government sites.

news.headline: Banks Left to Fend for Themselves During Outage
news.content: With government resources focused elsewhere, several banks struggled independently through the worst of the attack. Industry groups later called for a more coordinated national response framework going forward.

options.text: Order an immediate nationwide internet shutdown to stop the attack at its source
options.summary: Ordered a nationwide internet shutdown.

options.text: Wait for the attack to subside on its own before taking coordinated action
options.summary: Waited for the attack to subside without coordinated action.

title: Crisis Response
scenario: A serious vulnerability is discovered in the electronic identification cards used by most of the population for banking, voting, and government services. It could potentially be exploited before a patch is ready.
question: How do you manage this vulnerability?
learnMore: Estonia's 2017 eID crisis was resolved through the same core factors as 2007: clear recognition of the problem, transparent communication with the public about the risk, and a decisive patch rollout — rather than quietly hoping the vulnerability went unnoticed.

options.text: Disclose the vulnerability's existence and risk level to the public promptly while the patch is developed, with clear guidance on what to do meanwhile
options.summary: Disclosed the vulnerability promptly with clear public guidance.

news.headline: eID Vulnerability Disclosed, Patch Rollout Underway
news.content: Officials confirmed the vulnerability publicly and issued clear interim guidance for citizens, while a full patch was rolled out over following weeks. Security researchers praised the disclosure timeline as a model for future incidents.

options.text: Keep the vulnerability confidential until the patch is fully ready, telling no one in the meantime
options.summary: Kept the vulnerability confidential until the patch was ready.

news.headline: Silent Handling of eID Flaw Draws Criticism After the Fact
news.content: When the vulnerability became public after the patch was already deployed, opposition lawmakers questioned why citizens weren't warned earlier. Officials defended the approach as necessary to avoid panic, but public trust in digital ID took a measurable hit.

options.text: Suspend the entire eID system nationwide until the patch is ready
options.summary: Suspended the entire eID system during the patch process.

options.text: Deny the vulnerability exists until it can no longer be denied
options.summary: Denied the vulnerability's existence.

title: Resilience & Deterrence
scenario: The immediate incident has been resolved. Your team must now decide how much to invest in longer-term resilience versus returning attention to routine operations.
question: What's your approach to post-incident investment?
learnMore: A recurring lesson from Estonia's crisis management is continuous learning and investment in future cybersecurity — treating each incident as the basis for the next round of resilience-building, not a one-off event to move past quickly.

options.text: Commission a formal after-action review and commit multi-year funding to the resilience gaps it identifies
options.summary: Committed to multi-year resilience investment after a formal review.

options.text: Return to routine operations immediately with no formal review
options.summary: Returned to routine operations without a formal review.

options.text: Commission a review but leave its funding recommendations unimplemented
options.summary: Commissioned a review but left its recommendations unfunded.

options.text: Invest heavily in a single new technology without a broader resilience review
options.summary: Invested in a single new technology without a broader review.

title: Resilience & Deterrence
scenario: Prosecutors have secured convictions against several individuals recruited to carry out hybrid warfare activity, though key organisers remain fugitives abroad. You're asked how to message this outcome publicly.
question: What's your public messaging approach?
learnMore: In the real Seredenko and monument-vandalism cases, prosecutors publicly explained not just the verdicts but the underlying goal of the operations — creating fear, distrust, and instability — framing convictions as part of a broader pattern the public needed to understand, not isolated criminal cases.

options.text: Hold a public briefing explaining both the convictions and the broader pattern of hybrid operations they were part of
options.summary: Held a public briefing framing convictions within the broader pattern.

options.text: Announce only the legal outcome (sentences) with no explanation of the broader context
options.summary: Announced only the legal outcomes without context.

options.text: Keep the convictions out of the public record entirely to avoid drawing attention to the vulnerability that was exploited
options.summary: Kept the convictions out of public view entirely.

options.text: Use the briefing mainly to criticise the foreign government believed responsible, without addressing domestic resilience lessons
options.summary: Focused the briefing on blame rather than resilience lessons.

title: Nationwide DDoS Escalation
scenario: Without warning, a coordinated denial-of-service attack knocks major banks, news outlets, and government portals offline simultaneously, echoing Estonia's 2007 crisis. Citizens can't access services and rumours are spreading faster than facts.
question: How do you respond in the first critical hours?
learnMore: The 2007 Estonian DDoS attacks were, at the time, extremely disruptive — but the combination of fast recognition, transparent communication, and coordinated mitigation became the template still referenced in Estonian crisis response today.

options.text: Declare a coordinated national cyber-incident, activate all relevant agencies, and brief the public within the hour
options.summary: Declared a coordinated national incident and briefed the public quickly.

news.headline: Government Moves Fast as Nationwide Outage Hits
news.content: Within an hour of the first reports, officials confirmed a coordinated cyber-attack and outlined mitigation steps already underway. Public reaction was largely reassured by the speed and clarity of the response, even as some services remained intermittently down.

options.text: Wait several hours to gather more technical certainty before saying anything publicly
options.summary: Delayed public statement for hours during the outage.

news.headline: Hours of Silence Fuel Rumours During Outage
news.content: With no official statement for most of the day, social media filled the gap with speculation ranging from technical failure to full-scale cyberwar. When officials finally spoke, the delay itself became part of the story.

options.text: Publicly name a specific foreign government as responsible before any technical attribution is complete
options.summary: Named a foreign government as responsible before attribution was confirmed.

options.text: Instruct all affected institutions to handle the incident independently with no central coordination
options.summary: Left affected institutions to respond independently.

title: Digital ID Vulnerability Surfaces
scenario: Security researchers privately notify your office of a serious flaw in the national digital ID system that could allow identity theft at scale. No public exploitation has been detected yet, but the researchers plan to publish their findings in two weeks regardless.
question: How do you use the two-week window?
learnMore: This mirrors Estonia's 2017 eID crisis, where a vulnerability was discovered before large-scale exploitation. The response combined urgent patch development with transparent public communication once the risk was understood.

options.text: Fast-track an emergency patch, coordinate disclosure timing with the researchers, and prepare public guidance for the announcement
options.summary: Fast-tracked a patch and coordinated transparent disclosure timing.

news.headline: Digital ID Flaw Patched Ahead of Public Disclosure
news.content: Working closely with the researchers who found it, officials rolled out a fix before the vulnerability became public, then briefed citizens clearly on what happened and what to check. The coordinated approach was held up as a model for responsible disclosure.

options.text: Pressure the researchers to delay or cancel publication indefinitely
options.summary: Pressured researchers to delay publishing the vulnerability.

news.headline: Pressure Campaign Against Researchers Backfires Publicly
news.content: When word got out that officials had tried to suppress the disclosure, the story shifted from a technical vulnerability to a transparency scandal. The researchers published on schedule regardless, now with considerably more public attention.

options.text: Do nothing until the researchers publish, then respond reactively
options.summary: Took no action until after public disclosure.

options.text: Shut down the entire digital ID system immediately as a precaution
options.summary: Shut down the digital ID system as an immediate precaution.

title: Staged Monument Vandalism
scenario: War memorials across several towns are vandalised overnight with symbols designed to implicate domestic extremists. Investigators quickly suspect the vandals were recruited and directed by a foreign intelligence service, but the public narrative is already forming around 'homegrown extremism.'
question: How do you handle the investigation and public narrative simultaneously?
learnMore: This mirrors real 2023–24 cases where GRU-linked operatives recruited local individuals to vandalise memorials with instructions to fabricate evidence of domestic Nazi sympathies — intended to create fear, division, and distrust in domestic institutions.

options.text: Investigate thoroughly, and once foreign coordination is confirmed, explain both findings — the staged nature and the deeper intent — clearly to the public
options.summary: Investigated thoroughly and explained the staged nature once confirmed.

news.headline: Investigators Reveal Foreign Hand Behind Memorial Vandalism
news.content: After weeks of investigation, officials confirmed the vandalism was orchestrated by a foreign intelligence service using recruited locals. The disclosure shifted public conversation away from domestic blame and toward the actual source of the operation.

options.text: Let the 'domestic extremism' narrative stand publicly to avoid appearing to make excuses
options.summary: Let the domestic extremism narrative stand uncorrected.

options.text: Publicly blame the foreign government immediately, before the investigation is complete
options.summary: Publicly blamed a foreign government before investigation concluded.

options.text: Quietly close the case without any public explanation once suspects are identified
options.summary: Closed the case without public explanation.

title: Embassy-Funded 'Independent Expert'
scenario: A self-styled 'independent human rights expert,' whose travel is quietly funded by a foreign embassy, testifies at an international forum that your country's minority-language school reforms amount to 'language genocide.' The foreign ministry of that country immediately cites the testimony as proof of the claim.
question: What's your response?
learnMore: This is drawn directly from the real Seredenko case — a source-washing technique where a supposedly independent voice, secretly funded, delivers a claim that the funding government then cites back as if it were external validation.

options.text: Publish the funding evidence, note the term has no basis in international law, and formally respond at the same forum
options.summary: Published funding evidence and formally responded at the forum.

news.headline: Funding Ties Exposed for 'Independent Expert'
news.content: The revelation that the so-called independent expert's travel had been funded by a foreign embassy significantly undercut the credibility of his testimony among delegates, several of whom publicly noted the disclosure in follow-up statements.

options.text: Say nothing at the forum and address it only through domestic media afterward
options.summary: Addressed the claim only through domestic media, not the forum itself.

news.headline: Claim Goes Unanswered at International Forum
news.content: With no formal rebuttal delivered at the forum itself, the unchallenged testimony continued to circulate internationally for weeks before domestic officials addressed it — by which point it had already been cited in several follow-up articles abroad.

options.text: Attack the individual's personal credibility without addressing the funding or the substance of the claim
options.summary: Attacked the individual's credibility without addressing substance.

options.text: Formally protest to the forum organisers demanding the testimony be struck from the record
options.summary: Demanded the testimony be struck from the record.

title: Minister's Vehicle Targeted
scenario: The personal vehicle of a government minister — a vocal critic of a hostile foreign government's actions abroad — is vandalised, along with the home of a prominent local journalist. Investigators believe both are linked to the same foreign-recruited network behind recent memorial vandalism.
question: How do you respond to this escalation?
learnMore: Prosecutors in the real case explained that individuals targeted were vocal critics of foreign aggression, and that the broader intent was to create fear and panic, divert media attention, and disrupt support for the countries being criticised.

options.text: Increase protective measures for those targeted, pursue the investigation vigorously, and publicly name the pattern connecting the incidents once confirmed
options.summary: Increased protection and named the connected pattern once confirmed.

options.text: Treat each incident as an isolated case of vandalism with no broader pattern
options.summary: Treated the incidents as isolated and unconnected.

options.text: Advise the minister and journalist to lower their public profile to reduce further targeting
options.summary: Advised targeted individuals to lower their public profile.

options.text: Respond only privately to the minister without addressing the journalist's case or the public pattern
options.summary: Responded privately, leaving the broader pattern unaddressed.

title: Successful Prosecution Closes a Long-Running Case
scenario: After years of investigation, your security service secures a conviction against an individual proven to have cooperated with a foreign intelligence service for over a decade while posing as an independent civic voice.
question: How do you use this outcome?
learnMore: In the real Seredenko case, the individual was convicted after security services proved over a decade of cooperation with a foreign intelligence service — a result reached only through years of patient investigative work.

options.text: Publicise the case as a demonstration of investigative capability and use it to raise public awareness of source-washing tactics
options.summary: Publicised the conviction to raise awareness of source-washing tactics.

news.headline: Decade-Long Investigation Ends in Conviction
news.content: The successful prosecution, years in the making, was held up by officials as proof that patient investigative work pays off against long-running foreign influence operations. Analysts noted the case as a useful public case study in recognising similar tactics elsewhere.

options.text: Keep the case low-profile to avoid drawing attention to how long the activity went undetected
options.summary: Kept the successful prosecution low-profile.

options.text: Use the case mainly to criticise past leadership for not catching it sooner
options.summary: Used the case primarily to criticise past leadership.

title: NIS2 Compliance Comes Easily
scenario: An internal audit finds your country is already meeting most of the EU's NIS2 cybersecurity requirements, thanks to groundwork laid years earlier. Remaining gaps are minor.
question: What do you do with the freed-up resources and goodwill?
learnMore: In Estonia's case, many NIS2 parameters were already in place before the directive took effect, making compliance considerably easier than for member states starting from scratch.

options.text: Redirect freed-up resources toward longer-term resilience projects and offer to share lessons with countries further behind
options.summary: Redirected resources to resilience projects and shared lessons abroad.

news.headline: Early NIS2 Readiness Frees Resources for Resilience Work
news.content: With compliance largely already in hand, officials confirmed a shift in focus toward longer-term resilience investment, and announced plans to share implementation lessons with EU partners still working through the directive's requirements.

options.text: Redirect the resources to entirely unrelated government priorities
options.summary: Redirected freed-up resources to unrelated priorities.

options.text: Do nothing further since minimum compliance has technically been achieved
options.summary: Took no further action after achieving minimum compliance.

title: New Mitigation Technology Proves Effective
scenario: New DDoS mitigation technology deployed since the last major incident dramatically reduces disruption during a fresh attempted attack — services barely blink compared to the outages of years past.
question: How do you respond to this success?
learnMore: Lecture 2.3 notes that DDoS attacks, extremely disruptive in 2007, are far less disruptive today thanks to new mitigation technology — but also flags that new attack types like ransomware and AI-driven threats are emerging to take their place.

options.text: Publicly credit the investment while immediately turning attention to emerging threats like ransomware and AI-driven attacks
options.summary: Credited the success while pivoting focus to emerging threats.

news.headline: New Defences Hold Firm — Attention Turns to Next Threats
news.content: The near-nonevent of the latest attempted attack was widely seen as validation of recent infrastructure investment. Officials used the moment to announce a shift in focus toward newer threat categories, including ransomware and AI-enabled attacks.

options.text: Assume the DDoS threat is now fully solved and reduce related monitoring resources
options.summary: Reduced monitoring resources, assuming the threat was fully solved.

options.text: Keep the success entirely internal with no public acknowledgment
options.summary: Kept the successful mitigation entirely internal.
